thread.title: Market Volatility Bulletin: Stocks Work To Hold Wednesday's Outsized Gains

author: The Balance of Trade
title: Market Volatility Bulletin: Stocks Work To Hold Wednesday's Outsized Gains
text:
Market Intro
Source: CNBC - 1:06 PM EST
US stocks ( SPY , DIA , QQQ , IWM ) are on a rebound after a reasonably rough open on Thursday. Spot VIX has spent the day more or less in a one vol-point range.
Source: SectorSPDR
The sector breakdown for today is constructive to my way of thinking, insomuch as a lot of the large swings in equities have emanated from the tech ( XLK ), communications ( XLC ), financial ( XLF ) and discretionary ( XLY ) sectors.
Today, each of those sectors is in negative territory, and yet, at least for now, the S&P is holding up rather well.
This is the kind of behavior that tends to dampen volatility.
Oil ( USO ) continues to put on quite a show, and there remains a strong possibility that black gold puts in a dramatic showing over the next several weeks leading up to and then sorting out the OPEC meeting.
Thoughts on Volatility
I think the key here is that stocks seem to be looking for a reason to rally.
Clearly, the Powell meeting yesterday had a much greater effect on risk assets than the frenetic news tidbits surrounding trade terms between the US and China.
In setting up a bulletin rather than a "chat room," I wanted to essentially put out some ideas for other knowledgeable traders, learners and position takers to participate in and/or observe.
I do not believe that chat rooms are intrinsically bad, but I would like to caution readers against authoritative figures who speak in hyperbolic terms and otherwise sell the moon. There is no shortage of those in the field of investing and/or trading.
This is an important observation, echoed here . In a real sense, Powell was just making a factual claim rather than offering some kind of new, dovish guidance. My take is that he purposely took this route so as to perhaps gauge market reaction, while leaving plenty of room open to continue on the same course.
Term Structure
Certainly, I use Eli Mintz’s important volatility resource with regularity, and I am happy to feature it almost daily on the MVB . I second the shoutout to praise him for his hard work on a day where VIXcentral.com is experiencing technical difficulties.
Keep in mind that spot VIX is based on option vols on the SPX. According to this basket, the price of vol is $19.25, very near its historical average.
As ever, each of us is free to take either side of the trade. The key that I want to get at is that this is the market price of vol. I get the sense from reading others that all the market jitters are now out of the way...
Not according to this important metric. We should still be expecting meaningful moves - up and down - in the S&P 500 based on the current reading. We may, of course, see market volatility decline, but the forward-looking markets are not decisively taking that position.
Source: Google Finance
Same basic story - VIX9D has dropped (alongside spot) since the open, but this is a nine-day measure, and it's still quite high. Market participants may well have this story wrong, but the VIX9D could almost be described here as defiant.
Source: MarketChameleon.com - AAPL (green) vs. SPY (red) implied volatility
There is an important catalyst for a potential decline in volatility ( SVXY ). Note the significant push lower in Apple’s ( AAPL ) implied vol over the last week or so.
Remember that the tech behemoth, no longer the US’s most valuable company ( MSFT ), played an important role in fraying the market’s nerves over the last couple weeks.
A generalized departure from the price activity patterns at the top of the food chain is likely an important requirement to get S&P realized vol below 16 for any length of time.
Conclusion If this is your first time reading Market Volatility Bulletin, thanks for giving it a try. If you're a regular, we thank you for your ongoing contributions in the comments section.
Cool post, Hiro. I was happy to hear you describe some of your baseline assumptions regarding this market.
As a devil’s advocate perspective, bear markets can, and sometimes do, last for a long time. There’s a great quip about “burning itself out” from Burton Malkiel’s Random Walk Down Wall Street :
Investing is like making love to a gorilla: once you begin, you don’t stop when you want, you stop when the gorilla wants.
Thank you for reading.
